data.title: Meduza: In 1959, Nikita Khrushchev and Richard Nixon held one of the Cold War’s defining conversations: the ‘Kitchen Debate,’ inside a model American house at a Moscow exhibition
data.summary: In 1959, one of the most significant events of the Khrushchev Thaw took place in Moscow’s Sokolniki Park: the American National Exhibition. In its pavilions, Soviet citizens could explore American art and see how Americans lived: what cars they drove, what kitchens they cooked in, and what beds they slept in. But what the exhibition in Sokolniki is remembered for most is not its works of art and design, but the “Kitchen Debate.” On July 24, U.S. Vice President Richard Nixon arrived for the exhibition’s opening and met with Soviet Communist Party First Secretary Nikita Khrushchev. Together, the two toured a model American house that, according to its creators, any U.S. citizen could afford. When the two politicians stepped into the kitchen, Khrushchev had to make the case for the Soviet system while surrounded by unprecedented marvels: a refrigerator, a washing machine, and a dishwasher. Architecture journalist Asya Zolnikova tells the story of what that American house looked like, what else was at the Sokolniki exhibition, and what impact it had on U.S.-Russian relations.

At the turn of the century, the authorities often listened to lawyers and human rights advocates, and those advocates hoped Russia could build a fair justice system. Those hopes soon collapsed, and Bontsler and her colleagues watched as the state set about systematically dismantling human rights. After the full-scale war began, Bontsler took on cases involving “false information” and “discrediting the army,” until she herself was arrested in 2025. data.title: Meduza: ‘I’m not very interested in a hypothetical “democratic future for Russia.”’ Antiwar activist and former top model Ksenia Maksimova has more immediate priorities.
data.summary: At the end of September, Russian authorities put Ksenia Maksimova, head of the London-based antiwar group Russian Democratic Society (RDS), on an international wanted list. Shortly before that, she had been added to Russia’s registry of “terrorists and extremists,” and RDS had been declared an “undesirable” organization. Before entering politics, Maksimova worked as a top model and later as an agent for fashion photographers. She is now heavily involved in helping Ukraine (she even lives there), while also advocating for antiwar Russians in the British Parliament. In May 2026, she won a seat in London’s municipal elections, becoming a councilor for the borough of Ealing. Meduza spoke with Maksimova about life in London and Kyiv, Britain’s turn to the right, infighting in the opposition, and how to help Ukraine and antiwar Russians at the same time.
